title: The Big Ideas in The Essays of Montaigne
attribution: An original summary of the ideas in The Essays by Michel de Montaigne (1580). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher. If these ideas resonate, buy the full book.
summary:
Montaigne invented a form by admitting he had nothing to teach. At thirty-eight he retired to a tower on his family estate, intending to write about the classics, and produced instead a thousand pages about himself — his kidney stones, his memory, his fear of doctors, his dead friend, what he thinks about while riding. He called the pieces essais, meaning attempts or trials, and warned readers in the opening address that he was the subject of his own book and that they would be foolish to spend their leisure on so frivolous a matter.

That disclaimer is the innovation. Every writer before him wrote from authority. Montaigne writes from uncertainty, on purpose, and discovers that it is a far more reliable position.

# What do I know?

His motto was a question rather than a statement, and he had it struck on a medal: que sais-je. What do I know?

The scepticism is not a pose and not despair. It is a working method. He notices that the same act is a virtue in one country and a crime across the border, that what he believed firmly at twenty he finds absurd at fifty, that a fever changes his opinions more reliably than an argument does. From this he concludes not that truth is unavailable but that certainty is almost always premature, and that the people most confident are usually the least examined.

The practical effect on his writing is that he argues with himself in public and leaves the contradictions in. Later editions add material without deleting the passages the new material undermines, so you can watch a mind revise itself across twenty years on the same page.

# Custom is the thing you cannot see

His sharpest sociological insight is that habit does not merely influence judgment; it constitutes it. What we call natural is very often just local. He collects examples of practices that appear monstrous abroad and unremarkable at home, and turns the comparison back on his own society rather than treating foreigners as the curiosity.

In one of the most startling passages of the sixteenth century, he considers reports of cannibalism in the New World, grants that it is barbarous, and then observes that his own countrymen were at that moment tearing living men apart under the pretext of piety — which he judges worse than eating the dead. He is not excusing anything. He is refusing the exemption we grant ourselves by default.

# On the fear of death, and then the reversal

Montaigne spends a famous early essay arguing that to philosophise is to learn to die: keep death constantly in view, rehearse it, strip it of surprise, and you take away its power.

Then he changes his mind, which is the interesting part. After a riding accident left him unconscious and near death, he reported that the experience had been not agonising but gentle — he had drifted, felt no terror, and behaved calmly without any of the preparation he had recommended. His later position is close to the opposite of his earlier one: nature will teach you how to die at the moment required, the peasant manages it without a library, and a life spent rehearsing death is a life spent dying.

Few writers leave both arguments standing. He does, because the change is the evidence.

# Reading as a conversation with the dead

His attitude to books is the least reverent of any great reader's on record. He admits he reads for pleasure, abandons anything difficult, has a poor memory and forgets most of what he reads, and skips the parts that bore him. He would rather understand himself well than Cicero.

What he does instead of scholarship is conversation. He quotes constantly — hundreds of times, often without attribution, sometimes mangled from memory — but he uses the quotations as interlocutors rather than authorities, agreeing, arguing back, or letting a borrowed sentence say the thing he cannot say himself.

The lesson he draws is a warning about learning that never becomes anyone's. We take opinions into custody, he says, the way a man might carry someone else's coins in his purse and call himself rich. Knowledge only counts once it has changed how you judge, and that requires digesting it rather than storing it — which is precisely why forgetting most of a book is no disaster if the part that stayed did any work.

# The friendship at the centre

Underneath the whole project is a loss. Montaigne's closest friend, Étienne de La Boétie, died young, and the essays are in part a substitute for a conversation that ended. Asked to explain why the friendship was what it was, he refuses analysis and gives the line that has outlived every other in the book: because it was him, because it was me.

The refusal matters. He is willing to lose the explanation rather than falsify it, which is the same discipline he applies to himself throughout.

# Ordinary life, taken seriously

His conclusion, arrived at slowly across the last essays, is that the great and glorious masterpiece of humanity is to live appropriately — not to build empires, not to achieve ecstasy, but to be present in a plain day. He is scathing about people who despise ordinary existence in favour of some transcendent posture, and notes that even on the highest throne in the world we are still sitting on our own backside.

The advice that follows is unglamorous by design: keep company with your own thoughts, accept that your body is part of you rather than an inconvenience, distrust anyone who is never uncertain, and read for pleasure rather than for the appearance of having read.

# Why the form survived

Everything since — the personal essay, the column, the memoir that thinks, most good blogging — descends from a man who decided that the honest report of one ordinary mind was worth more than a confident report about the universe.

The risk of the form is obvious and he names it: nobody has any reason to care about his kidney stones. His answer is that he is not offering himself as remarkable but as a specimen, and that each man bears the entire form of the human condition. Read enough of one person, closely and without flattery, and you are reading about everyone.
